passages.happening:
‘Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem fifty-five years’ (verse 1). ‘And he did evil in the sight of the LORD by following the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites’ (verse 2). He rebuilds the high places his father had torn down, raises altars for the Baals, makes Asherah poles and worships the host of heaven (verse 3). He builds altars in both courtyards of the house of the LORD (verses 4-5).

‘He sacrificed his sons in the fire in the Valley of Hinnom’ (verse 6). He practices sorcery and divination and consults mediums. He sets a carved image in the house of God, the place God had chosen for his Name forever (verse 7), and leads Judah to do ‘greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites’ (verse 9). ‘And the LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they did not listen’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Hezekiah was among the best of David's heirs; his son begins as the worst. Chronicles lists his sins at length because they are the very abominations for which the land's earlier peoples lost it, and the temple Hezekiah cleansed becomes a gallery of idols.

Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, the longest of any king of Judah, commonly placed about 697 to 642 BC, possibly including years beside his father. These were the decades of Assyria's greatest power under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, and inscriptions of both kings list Manasseh of Judah among the western rulers who sent tribute or building materials. Judah was a loyal vassal through most of this time.

The host of heaven was the sun, moon and stars worshiped as gods, a practice widespread in Mesopotamia. Sorcery, divination and consulting mediums were forbidden by the law because they sought hidden knowledge and power apart from God. The carved image, semel, was probably an image of Asherah. Verse 6 names child sacrifice, the deepest evil a king could do. The text names it, and these notes do not describe it.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: Second Kings adds, ‘Moreover, Manasseh shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem from end to end’ (2 Kings 21:16).
passages.asks: The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, and they did not listen. Ask what God has been saying to you that you have not wanted to hear. And ask what the people who follow you are learning from your example.

passages.t: In his distress, Manasseh humbles himself
passages.happening:
‘So the LORD brought against them the military commanders of the king of Assyria, who captured Manasseh, put a hook in his nose, bound him with bronze shackles, and took him to Babylon’ (verse 11). ‘And in his distress, Manasseh sought the favor of the LORD his God and earnestly humbled himself before the God of his fathers’ (verse 12). ‘And when he prayed to Him, the LORD received his plea and heard his petition; so He brought him back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God’ (verse 13).

He rebuilds the outer wall of the City of David and stations commanders in the fortified cities (verse 14). ‘He removed the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, along with all the altars he had built on the temple mount and in Jerusalem, and he dumped them outside the city’ (verse 15). He restores the altar of the LORD and tells Judah to serve the LORD (verse 16). ‘Nevertheless, the people still sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God’ (verse 17). His prayer is written in the records of the seers (verses 18-19), and he is buried at his palace (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is built on reversal. Verse 10 is the hinge: the LORD spoke and they did not listen. Then come punishment and prayer, and verses 14 to 17 reverse the earlier sins one by one: the idol removed, the altars thrown out, the LORD's altar restored. The hook in the nose and bronze shackles were real practices; Assyrian reliefs show captives led by ropes on rings, and the prophets use the image of a hook for Assyria's own humiliation. Rebuilding walls and stationing commanders fits a vassal restored and trusted to guard a frontier.

The key words are kana, to humble oneself, and atar, to plead, which also describes God's willingness to be pleaded with. Knew, yada, in Hebrew means knowledge gained by experience. The whole chapter acts out God's words in 7:14: a people who humble themselves, pray, seek and turn.

For the Chronicler's first readers, back from exile in Babylon, the story had special force. If God heard Manasseh in Babylon and brought him home, he could hear them too. A later Jewish prayer called the Prayer of Manasseh is printed in some Bibles among the Apocrypha, but most scholars date it much later, so it is not the text verses 18 and 19 cite.
passages.later: Second Kings says of the fall of Jerusalem that it came ‘because of the sins of Manasseh and all that he had done’ (2 Kings 24:3), and ‘the LORD was unwilling to forgive’ (2 Kings 24:4).
passages.hard:
Second Kings blames Manasseh for the exile and says nothing of his repentance. Why does Chronicles tell a different story, and which is true?

The two books tell the story for different purposes, and readers account for the difference in more than one way, each in its own terms.

Kings, completed during the exile, explains why Jerusalem fell, and it names Manasseh's sins and the innocent blood he shed as the tipping point. It tells his reign without any captivity or repentance. When Kings says the LORD was unwilling to forgive, that concerns the verdict on Jerusalem as a city and a kingdom; it does not set a limit on God's mercy toward anyone who turns to him.

Chronicles, written after the return, shows its readers that repentance is always possible and that God hears those who humble themselves. Some historians think the Chronicler used a reliable source unknown to the writer of Kings, pointing to the records of the seers he names in verse 19. They note that Assyrian records list Manasseh among the vassal kings of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, and some connect a summons to Babylon with Assyria's efforts to secure loyalty in the west during a Babylonian revolt against Ashurbanipal in the 650s BC, when Assyria ruled Babylon. Others remain cautious, since no Assyrian text mentions the event. Others think the Chronicler shaped Manasseh's long reign into a lesson about repentance, perhaps building on a real deportation.

The two accounts can be true together. Manasseh's own repentance did not undo the damage his decades of idolatry had done to the nation, as Amon's quick return to idols shows, and the people still worshiped at the high places. Kings tells the cost to the nation; Chronicles tells the mercy to the man. The site's notes on 2 Kings 21 say the same and take no side on the history.
passages.asks: The worst king of Judah prayed in chains and was heard. Ask whether you believe anyone is beyond God's hearing, yourself included. And ask what damage you have done that your own repentance cannot undo, and who might need you to help repair it.

passages.t: Amon, who did not humble himself
passages.happening: ‘Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem two years’ (verse 21). He does evil as his father had done and sacrifices to all his father's idols, ‘but he did not humble himself before the LORD as his father Manasseh had done; instead, Amon increased his guilt’ (verse 23). His servants conspire and kill him in his palace, and the people of the land kill the conspirators and make his son Josiah king (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
Amon's short reign is a mirror. He copied his father's sin but not his father's repentance, and the Chronicler uses the same verb to say so: he did not humble himself. Amon ruled about 642 to 640 BC. His death brings the boy Josiah to the throne.

The contrast is the point. Repentance is not inherited, and neither is ruin. Each generation stands before God on its own account.
passages.later: Second Kings tells the same end: ‘Then the servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his palace’ (2 Kings 21:23).
passages.asks: Amon learned his father's sins and not his father's repentance. Ask what the next generation is learning from you, your failures or your turning. And ask whether you have let them see you humble yourself.
